[1-3] ﴿Ha Mim.﴾ ﴿By the Book that makes things clear.﴾ ﴿Indeed We sent it down on a blessed night; indeed We were ever warning.﴾

He means the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr), in which He, glorified be He, decreed the sending down of His wise Reminder. The discourse on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[4] ﴿In it every matter of wisdom is made distinct.﴾

﴿In it every matter of wisdom is made distinct.﴾ That is: every matter that wisdom requires is separated out and made clear, in a manner that is firm and praiseworthy according to the perfected ones (al-kummal), by which their spirits are nourished and their souls are shown mercy. And His words, may He be exalted:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[5, 6] ﴿A command from Us. Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾ ﴿as a mercy from your Lord. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Dukhan: 5–6].

﴿A command from Us﴾ is in the accusative by way of *al-ikhtisas* (specification, a construction in which a noun is singled out for emphasis). That is: I mean by this matter a command originating from Us, in accordance with Our decree. This explains its grandeur in relation to Us, after the explanation of its grandeur in itself: ﴿Indeed, We were ever sending [messengers]﴾ ﴿as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Dukhan: 6]. That is, We were sending messengers to mankind, a Messenger from among themselves who recites to them the signs of God, purifies them, and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom, as a mercy from Him, exalted is He, toward them, because of the pressing need for him, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 107]. It is also permitted that "mercy" be the cause (*'illah*) of the sending down. That is: a complete and perfect mercy upon the worlds through its sending down, for the rectitude of their religious and worldly affairs, the soundness of their livelihood and their final destiny, and the appearance among them, by means of it, of goodness, perfection, blessing, and right guidance.

The first interpretation is the more correct, namely that it is the purpose (*ghayah*) of the sending, since that verse explicitly states it. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ [al-Dukhan: 6], that is, to the calls of the realities of things according to their requirements; ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Dukhan: 6], that is, to the measures of their capacities. Therefore, sending and sending down are not far from Him. This is what al-Mahayimi said.

Al-Qashani said: That is, the All-Hearing of their various statements concerning religious matters that proceed from their desires; the All-Knowing: of their false beliefs, their corrupt opinions, their various affairs, and their disordered livelihoods. For this reason He showed them mercy by sending the Messenger who guides to the truth in matters of religion, who organizes their interests in worldly matters, who directs them to what is right in both, by clarifying the straight path, establishing the Oneness of God through proof, and legislating the laws and the norms of rulings to secure order.

al-Qasimi's commentary (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 44, verses 10–12:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[10–12] ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke, covering the people. This is a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11] ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12]

﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke, covering the people. This is a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11] ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12] That is: wait for their recompense on that terrifying Day. The verb (al-irtiqab, "watching/waiting") is used only for something disliked. Regarding the meaning of "smoke," the early generations (al-salaf) had three views.

The first: Some of them said: This was when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against Quraysh that they be struck with years like the years of Yusuf, and so they were struck with famine. They said: By the "smoke" is meant what affected their eyesight at that time from the severity of hunger, a darkness like the appearance of smoke. Ibn Jarir narrated from Masruq, who said: "We were sitting with Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and he was reclining among us. A man came to him and said: 'O Abu Abd al-Rahman, a storyteller at the doors of Kinda is telling tales and claims that the sign of the smoke will come and seize the breaths of the disbelievers, and it will seize the believers in a manner like a cold.' He said: 'O people! Fear Allah. Whoever knows something, let him say what he knows; and whoever does not know, let him say: "Allah knows best." For it is part of knowledge that a person says of what he does not know: "Allah knows best." Nor should anyone say of what he does not know: "I do not know." For Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it, and I am not of those who pretend.﴾ [Sad: 86].' When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw the people turning away, he said: «O Allah, seven years like the seven years of Yusuf.» So a year of drought struck them that consumed everything, until they ate hides, carrion and corpses. One of them would look at the sky and see smoke because of the hunger."

Abu Sufyan ibn Harb came to him and said: "O Muhammad! You came commanding us to obey and to maintain the ties of kinship, and your people have perished, so invoke Allah for them." Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed you will return [to disbelief].﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. He said: "Then it was removed from them": ﴿The Day We will strike the greatest blow; indeed We will take retribution.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]. So "the blow" was on the Day of Badr. The "smoke" verse, the "Rum" verse, the "blow," and the "grip" have passed.

Ibn Kathir said: This hadith is narrated in the "Two Sahihs" (al-Sahihayn), and Imam Ahmad narrated it in his "Musnad," and it is in al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i in their "Tafsirs," and in Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim through multiple chains. The view that the verse refers to this, and that the smoke has already passed, agrees with Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and was held by a group of the early generations, such as Mujahid, Abu al-Aliya, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak and Ata' al-Awfi, and it is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in (al-Fath): The apparent view is that Abu Sufyan's visit occurred before the Hijrah, due to Ibn Mas'ud's saying: "then they returned." It is not reported that Abu Sufyan came to Madinah before Badr. On this basis, it is possible that Abu Talib was present at that event, and therefore he said:

*And a white one, by whose face rain-clouds are sought.*

However, there are reports indicating that the mentioned story occurred in Madinah. If it is not taken to be a repeated event, then it is very problematic. And Allah is the One sought for help. End of quotation.

Ibn Qutayba, in interpreting the smoke according to this view, mentioned two meanings:

The first: that in a year of drought, the dryness of the land greatly increases because rain stops, great dust rises, and the air becomes dark. That resembles smoke, and for this reason a year of famine is called "al-Ghabra" (the dusty one).

The second: that the Arabs call a prevailing evil "smoke," so they say: "There was a matter between us, from which smoke rose." The reason for this is that when a person's fear or weakness intensifies, his eyes darken, so he sees the world as if filled with smoke. End of quotation.

Al-Shihab said: The apparent view is that this naming is a metaphor, because smoke is something that harms, so it is applied to every harmful thing resembling it, or to what it entails. For this reason it was said:

*You seek a refined one without any fault... but is there a wood that gives off fragrance without smoke?*

(The second view regarding the verse:) It is that it is a smoke that appears in the world, one of the signs of the Hour, which has not yet come, but will come. This is the view of Hudhayfah, and it is reported from Ali, Ibn Abbas, and a group of the Successors (al-Tabi'un). Al-Razi said: Those who held this view argued with several points:

The first: His saying, "the Day the sky will bring smoke," requires the existence of a smoke that the sky brings. What you have mentioned, the darkness that occurs in the eye because of the severity of hunger, is not smoke brought by the sky. So interpreting the wording of the verse in this way is a departure from its apparent meaning without a separate proof, and that is not permissible.

The second: He described that smoke as "visible," and the condition you mentioned is not so; for it is an incidental affliction that happens to some people in their brains, and such a thing is not described as a visible smoke.

The third: He described that smoke as one that "covers the people." This is true only if that smoke reaches them and envelops them, whereas the condition you mentioned covers people only figuratively, and we have stated that departing from the literal to the figurative is not permissible without a separate proof.

The fourth: what has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) counting the smoke among the awaited signs. As for those who hold the first view, there is no doubt that this requires turning the word from its literal meaning to a figurative one, and that is not permissible except when there is proof that its literal meaning is impossible; and these people have not mentioned that proof. So their position, as they stated it, is very problematic. If they say: the proof that what we mentioned is intended is that He, exalted is He, related about them that they say: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12], and this is consistent if we take it to refer to the famine that occurred in Makkah. For it is reported that when the famine became severe in Makkah, Abu Sufyan went to him and pleaded with him by Allah and by kinship, and promised that if he invoked for them and Allah removed that calamity from them, they would believe in him. When Allah, exalted is He, removed that from them, they returned to their polytheism.

As for if we take it to mean that it is one of the signs of the Hour, that cannot be valid, because at the appearance of the signs of the Hour they cannot say: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12], and it is also not valid to say to them: ﴿Indeed We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return [to disbelief].﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. The answer: Why is it not permissible that the appearance of this sign should be like the appearance of the rest of the signs of the Hour, in that it does not necessitate the cessation of obligation, so this condition occurs? Then people fear greatly and humble themselves. When that event passes, they return to disbelief and wickedness. And if this is possible, then what they have said falls away. And Allah knows best. End of the words of al-Razi.

Thus Imam Ibn Kathir preferred the second view, following what is authentically reported from Ibn Abbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, and those among the Companions and Successors who agreed with him, together with the sound and fair (hasan) raised (marfu') hadiths and others that they cited, which give conviction and clear indication that the smoke is one of the awaited signs. Moreover, it is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾, meaning: clear and evident, which everyone sees. As for what Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, interpreted, it is merely an imagining they saw in their eyes from the severity of hunger and hardship. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿covering the people﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11], meaning: it envelops them and includes them all. And if it were an imagined matter specific to the polytheists of Makkah, it would not have been said of it: ﴿covering the people﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11], meaning: it will be said to them, as a rebuke and reproach, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed into the fire of Hell with a violent push. This is the Fire which you used to deny.﴾ [al-Tur: 13–14], or some of them will say this to others.

And His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12], meaning: the disbelievers will say, when they witness the punishment of Allah and His retribution, asking for its lifting and removal from them, as in His saying, may His greatness be exalted: ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire and they say: "Oh, if only we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers."﴾ [al-An'am: 27], and likewise His saying, may He be majestic and high: ﴿Warn the people of the Day when the punishment will come to them, and those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, delay us for a short term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." Did you not swear before that there would be no decline for you?﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. Thus did He, may His majesty be great, say.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw the people turning away, he said: «O Allah, seven years like the seven years of Yusuf.» So a year of drought struck them that consumed everything, until they ate hides, carrion and corpses. One of them would look at the sky and see smoke because of the hunger."

Abu Sufyan ibn Harb came to him and said: "O Muhammad! You came commanding us to obey and to maintain the ties of kinship, and your people have perished, so invoke Allah for them." Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed you will return [to disbelief].﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. He said: "Then it was removed from them": ﴿The Day We will strike the greatest blow; indeed We will take retribution.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]. So "the blow" was on the Day of Badr. The "smoke" verse, the "Rum" verse, the "blow," and the "grip" have passed.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in (al-Fath): The apparent view is that Abu Sufyan's visit occurred before the Hijrah, due to Ibn Mas'ud's saying: "then they returned." It is not reported that Abu Sufyan came to Madinah before Badr. On this basis, it is possible that Abu Talib was present at that event, and therefore he said:

*And a white one, by whose face rain-clouds are sought.*

However, there are reports indicating that the mentioned story occurred in Madinah. If it is not taken to be a repeated event, then it is very problematic. And Allah is the One sought for help. End of quotation.

Ibn Qutayba, in interpreting the smoke according to this view, mentioned two meanings:

The first: that in a year of drought, the dryness of the land greatly increases because rain stops, great dust rises, and the air becomes dark. That resembles smoke, and for this reason a year of famine is called "al-Ghabra" (the dusty one).

The second: that the Arabs call a prevailing evil "smoke," so they say: "There was a matter between us, from which smoke rose." The reason for this is that when a person's fear or weakness intensifies, his eyes darken, so he sees the world as if filled with smoke. End of quotation.

Al-Shihab said: The apparent view is that this naming is a metaphor, because smoke is something that harms, so it is applied to every harmful thing resembling it, or to what it entails. For this reason it was said:

*You seek a refined one without any fault... but is there a wood that gives off fragrance without smoke?*

(The second view regarding the verse:) It is that it is a smoke that appears in the world, one of the signs of the Hour, which has not yet come, but will come. This is the view of Hudhayfah, and it is reported from Ali, Ibn Abbas, and a group of the Successors (al-Tabi'un). Al-Razi said: Those who held this view argued with several points:

The first: His saying, "the Day the sky will bring smoke," requires the existence of a smoke that the sky brings. What you have mentioned, the darkness that occurs in the eye because of the severity of hunger, is not smoke brought by the sky. So interpreting the wording of the verse in this way is a departure from its apparent meaning without a separate proof, and that is not permissible.

The second: He described that smoke as "visible," and the condition you mentioned is not so; for it is an incidental affliction that happens to some people in their brains, and such a thing is not described as a visible smoke.

The third: He described that smoke as one that "covers the people." This is true only if that smoke reaches them and envelops them, whereas the condition you mentioned covers people only figuratively, and we have stated that departing from the literal to the figurative is not permissible without a separate proof.

The fourth: what has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) counting the smoke among the awaited signs. As for those who hold the first view, there is no doubt that this requires turning the word from its literal meaning to a figurative one, and that is not permissible except when there is proof that its literal meaning is impossible; and these people have not mentioned that proof. So their position, as they stated it, is very problematic. If they say: the proof that what we mentioned is intended is that He, exalted is He, related about them that they say: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12], and this is consistent if we take it to refer to the famine that occurred in Makkah. For it is reported that when the famine became severe in Makkah, Abu Sufyan went to him and pleaded with him by Allah and by kinship, and promised that if he invoked for them and Allah removed that calamity from them, they would believe in him. When Allah, exalted is He, removed that from them, they returned to their polytheism.

As for if we take it to mean that it is one of the signs of the Hour, that cannot be valid, because at the appearance of the signs of the Hour they cannot say: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12], and it is also not valid to say to them: ﴿Indeed We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return [to disbelief].﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. The answer: Why is it not permissible that the appearance of this sign should be like the appearance of the rest of the signs of the Hour, in that it does not necessitate the cessation of obligation, so this condition occurs? Then people fear greatly and humble themselves. When that event passes, they return to disbelief and wickedness. And if this is possible, then what they have said falls away. And Allah knows best. End of the words of al-Razi.

Thus Imam Ibn Kathir preferred the second view, following what is authentically reported from Ibn Abbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, and those among the Companions and Successors who agreed with him, together with the sound and fair (hasan) raised (marfu') hadiths and others that they cited, which give conviction and clear indication that the smoke is one of the awaited signs. Moreover, it is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾, meaning: clear and evident, which everyone sees. As for what Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, interpreted, it is merely an imagining they saw in their eyes from the severity of hunger and hardship. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿covering the people﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11], meaning: it envelops them and includes them all. And if it were an imagined matter specific to the polytheists of Makkah, it would not have been said of it: ﴿covering the people﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 11], meaning: it will be said to them, as a rebuke and reproach, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed into the fire of Hell with a violent push. This is the Fire which you used to deny.﴾ [al-Tur: 13–14], or some of them will say this to others.

And His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12], meaning: the disbelievers will say, when they witness the punishment of Allah and His retribution, asking for its lifting and removal from them, as in His saying, may His greatness be exalted: ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand before the Fire and they say: "Oh, if only we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers."﴾ [al-An'am: 27], and likewise His saying, may He be majestic and high: ﴿Warn the people of the Day when the punishment will come to them, and those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, delay us for a short term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." Did you not swear before that there would be no decline for you?﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. Thus did He, may His majesty be great, say.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[15] ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return (to disbelief).﴾

﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return.﴾ This admits of two meanings:

The first: He, exalted is He, says: "Even if We removed the punishment from you and returned you to the worldly abode, you would return to what you were in of disbelief and denial." Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And even if We had mercy upon them and removed what harm is upon them, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 75] And like His saying, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾ [al-An'am: 28]

The second: that the intended meaning is, "Indeed, We will delay the punishment from you a little after its causes have been established and it has reached you, while you remain persistent in the transgression and misguidance you are in." The removal from them does not necessarily mean that it had touched them. Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except the people of Yunus; when they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time.﴾ [Yunus: 98] The punishment had not touched them or reached them; rather, its cause had been established upon them. Nor does it necessarily follow that they had ceased from their disbelief and then returned to it. Allah, exalted is He, related, informing about Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, that he said to his people when they said: ﴿O Shu'ayb, we will surely expel you and those who believed with you from our town, or you will return to our religion.' He said, 'Even if we were unwilling?'﴾ [al-A'raf: 88] ﴿We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah had saved us from it.﴾ [al-A'raf: 89] And Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, had never been upon their religion or their way. Qatadah said: ﴿Indeed, you will return﴾ to the punishment of Allah. And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

The discussion of the words of God Almighty:

[16] ﴿On the day when We shall strike the greatest striking; indeed, We will take retribution.﴾

﴿On the day when We shall strike the greatest striking; indeed, We will take retribution.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, explained this as the Day of Badr. This is the view of a group who agreed with Ibn Mas'ud in his interpretation of the smoke as mentioned earlier. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, through the narration of al-'Awfi from him. And from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, and a group from him, and it is plausible. The apparent meaning is that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, although the Day of Badr was also a day of striking.

Ibn Jarir said: Ya'qub related to me. Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us. Khalid al-Hadhdha' related to us from 'Ikrimah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The greatest striking is the Day of Badr." And I say it is the Day of Resurrection. This is a sound chain of narration from him. And al-Hasan al-Basri holds this view, as does 'Ikrimah in the more authentic of the two narrations from him. And Allah knows best. The words of Ibn Kathir end.

Section:

Among those who preferred the first interpretation, namely that the smoke refers metaphorically to the day of famine and hardship, by mentioning the cause and intending the effect, or by metaphor, is the Allamah Abu al-Su'ud, where he said: "The first is what the noble context definitely calls for; for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿How will they have the reminder?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13] and so on, is a rejection of their words and their demand for the removal (of the punishment), and a denial of their promise of faith, which indicates remembrance and admonition by the calamity that befell them; that is: how can they remember? Or from where would they remember this and fulfil what they promised of faith when the punishment is lifted from them? ﴿And a clear messenger had already come to them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13], that is, while they had witnessed the causes of remembrance and the requirements of admonition that are greater than it in bringing them about, since there came to them a messenger of great stature, who showed them the paths of truth, by manifesting clear signs and overpowering miracles, before which the deaf mountains would fall prostrate.

﴿Then they turned away from him﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14], from that messenger, though he is the same one, for a while, despite witnessing from him the great things that require turning towards him, and they were not content with turning away. ﴿And they said﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14] about him: ﴿A taught one, a madman﴾ [al-Dukhan: 14], that is: at one time they said, "He is taught by a foreign slave of some Thaqif," and at another, "He is mad," or some of them say one thing and others say something else. So can one expect from a people with these attributes that they be affected by admonition and reminder? Their likeness is only that of the dog: if it is hungry it is weak, and if it is satisfied it becomes insolent."

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15] is an answer from Him, Exalted is He, to their words: ﴿Our Lord, remove from us the punishment; indeed, we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12], by way of iltifat (turning of address), for greater rebuke and threat, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. That is: Indeed, We will remove the known punishment from you, a little removal, or for a short time. Indeed, you will return immediately after that to what you were upon of arrogance and persistence in disbelief, and you will forget this state. The purpose of restricting it with His saying "a little" is to indicate the increase of their wickedness, since if they return before the complete removal, they will be quicker to return after it. The use of the active participle form in both verbs is to indicate that both will certainly occur, and indeed both occurred when Allah removed it through the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ, and they soon returned to what they had been upon of arrogance and obstinacy. The end of what Abu al-Su'ud said, with additions.

Section:

As for the third interpretation of the verse, Ibn Abi Hatim said: Ubayy related to us, Ja'far ibn Musafir related to us. Yahya ibn Hassan related to us. Ibn Mahay'a related to us. 'Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj related to us concerning His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿On the day when the sky brings a manifest smoke﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10], he said: It was the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Ibn Kathir said: This statement is very strange, indeed rejected. The end.

That is: because it has not been reported either as marfu' or as mawquf from Ibn 'Abbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, or others of the Companions. However, the absence of its being transmitted does not negate the possibility of the wording of the verse bearing it and its applicability to it, especially since His saying at the end of the surah supports it: ﴿So wait; indeed, they are waiting﴾ [al-Dukhan: 59], which is a promise of His victory over them, and that was the day of the Conquest. In that case, the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15] is: what will descend upon them that day, by lifting killing and captivity from them. And the meaning of ﴿you will return﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15] is: to the meeting with Allah and His recompense.

Section:

From what we have transmitted from the early generations regarding this verse among the three sayings, it appears that this verse is among those verses which the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, took up with great concern for its meaning and careful research into what is intended by it, to the point that Ibn Mas'ud insisted on one interpretation, while 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and Hudhayfah held another, as is reported from them through various chains. By the truth of my life! This verse is indeed worthy of greater attention. And so is every matter that has been a battleground of views among the great imams. The cause of the disagreement is the concise style of the noble discourse and its preference for the most delicate and concise words, which truly admit of both literal and metaphorical meaning in its eloquence. This is the first point.

Second: since many of the transmitted hadiths resemble the verses, this brings them closer together and calls for uniting the intended meaning of both. This is because the Sunnah's explanation of the Book is established, and this is the path followed by the hadith scholars entirely. So you find one of them, when he sees in a report something that alludes to a verse, he asserts that it is its explanation and stops there without going beyond it. As for one who opened the door to reflection, paved the way for consideration, and saw that the report may be among the implications and instances of the verse, and that the verse is more general and comprehensive, or that applying the report to it is a confusion arising from similarity, then that person has widened the paths for the traveller and opened the faculties for the seeker, and elevated him from the enclosure of transmission to the expanse of reason. Each has his direction.

Having known this, you see that whoever interprets this verse as the famine which befell the Quraysh, it is possible for him to apply the verse to it metaphorically in some of its terms, and literally in the rest, and in its being the fulfilment of its reality in his view. Whoever interprets it as the awaited smoke, transmitted as one of the portents of the Hour, stands with the transmitted report and sees it as its explanation, because the default is agreement and reference to what is known, since that is the closest to occurring to the mind and the first to come to presence. Whoever interprets it as their being overcome on the day of the Conquest sees it as among the eloquent metaphor and the wonderful metonymy in that, and that the promise of waiting has many similar examples and parallels in more than one verse, meaning the Conquest, such as the verse: ﴿They say: When is this victory, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 28]; ﴿Say: On the day of victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be reprieved﴾ [al-Sajdah: 29]; ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed, they are waiting﴾ [al-Sajdah: 30].

This and its like clarify the sources and bases of the imams in interpretation. And by it it is known that the ends of the bases may pull on the wording, so that the opinion is held back from inclining to one basis rather than another, unless there is something that favours one of them. The one who reads al-Razi's earlier discussion and his argument for the second view, at such length, may think there is no escape from it. Yet whoever holds another view may answer his argument by what we have already mentioned about the validity of metaphor, indeed its strength here, because the context is one of warning and threat, and taste is the greatest judge, and to it returns the measure of eloquence. The interpreter is not obliged to deny the awaited smoke, as may be supposed; rather, he recognises it as a coming sign on the day when the earth is changed into other than the earth and the heavens, and this order is transformed into a second creation. And it does not follow from verbal homonymy that the recited and the transmitted are one and the same.

In sum, the noble wording encompasses the three meanings, and the reason is the realisation of the fulfilment of all of them. As for determining one of them as the intended meaning, it is very difficult in my view, especially since the Companions did not agree on one opinion about it. This is what we say now. And Allah is the All-Knowing. And His saying, Exalted is He:

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[17] ﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble Messenger﴾.

﴿And We had already tested before them the people of Pharaoh﴾: that is, We tried them, before these polytheists, the people of Pharaoh, by sending Moses, upon him be peace, to them so that they would believe. [29] ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them, nor were they given respite.﴾

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: When a man of high standing dies, the Arabs, to magnify his loss, would say: "The heaven and the earth wept for him, the wind wept for him, and the sun was darkened for him." Jarir said:

*"The stars of the night and the moon weep over you."*

(p-5308) The Kharijite woman (a woman of the Khawarij, a early sect) said:

*"O tree of al-Khabur, why are you in leaf, as if you did not grieve for Ibn Tarif?"*

This is by way of figurative representation and imagination (al-tamthil wal-takhyil), in emphasis of the obligation of grief and weeping for him. Likewise is what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, about the prayer-place of the believer weeping, and his traces on the earth, the ascent of his deeds, and the descent of his provision from the heaven: it is figurative. The negation of this for them, in His saying, ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep for them﴾, carries mockery of them and of their condition, which contradicts the condition of one whose loss is great, of whom it is said: "The heaven and the earth wept for him." That is: the people of the heaven and the people of the earth did not weep for them. ﴿Nor were they given respite﴾, meaning: they were not delayed in punishment. [34, 35] ﴿Indeed, these ones say﴾ ﴿"There is not but our first death, and we will not be resurrected."﴾ [al-Dukhan: 35].

﴿Indeed, these ones﴾, that is, the polytheists of Quraysh, ﴿say﴾ ﴿"There is not but our first death"﴾ [al-Dukhan: 35], that is, the one that follows life, as though they meant: "There is nothing but this death of ours." This was mentioned by a group of scholars, among them al-Wahidi in his tafsir, and al-Zajjaj. Among the branches of this question is that if someone says: "If the first child you bear is a male, then you are divorced," she is divorced when she gives birth to him, even if she bears no other, by consensus. [36] ﴿So bring back our fathers, if you are truthful.﴾

﴿So bring back our fathers, if you are truthful.﴾ That is: (bring them back) to resurrect us after our decay in our graves. Ibn Kathir said: This is a false argument and a corrupt doubt, for the Resurrection (ma'ad) is only on the Day of Judgment, not in the abode of this world. Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[37] ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals.﴾

﴿Are they better﴾: that is, in strength and power. ﴿Or the people of Tubba' and those before them? We destroyed them, for they were criminals﴾: that is, We destroyed them for their crime, which was their disbelief and corruption. And they were what they were. So what is the matter with Quraysh that they do not fear that what befell them may befall her?

The people of Tubba' were Himyar and the people of Saba'. Allah, mighty and majestic, destroyed them and scattered them throughout the lands, utterly dispersed, as has passed in Surat Saba'. Ibn Kathir said: They were Arabs from Qahtan, just as these are Arabs from 'Adnan. Himyar, whenever a man ruled over them, called him Tubba' (a title meaning "successor"), just as (Kisra) is said of the one who ruled the Persians, (Qaysar) of the one who ruled the Romans, (Fir'awn) of the one who ruled Egypt as an unbeliever, and (al-Najashi) of the one who ruled Abyssinia, and other such titles of peoples.

It so happened that one of their Tubba's went out from Yemen and travelled through the lands until he reached Samarqand. His kingdom grew strong, his authority and army became great, his realm and lands expanded, and his subjects multiplied. He is the one who founded al-Hirah. It so happened that he passed by the Prophet's city (Madinah), in the days of the Jahiliyyah. He intended to fight its people, but they resisted him and fought him by day, and by night they would feed him (hospitality). He was ashamed before them and refrained from them, and he took with him two rabbis of the Jews, who had advised him and informed him that he had no way over this town, for it is the place of emigration of a Prophet who will appear at the end of time. So he turned back from it and took the two with him to the land of Yemen. When he passed by Makkah he intended to demolish the Ka'bah, but they forbade him from that also, and they informed him of the greatness of (p-5311) this House, that it was built by Ibrahim the Friend, upon him be blessings and peace, and that it would have a great station at the hands of that Prophet who would be sent at the end of time. So he glorified it, circumambulated it, and clothed it with coverings, mantles and striped garments. Then he returned to Yemen and called its people to Judaism along with him. At that time the religion of Musa, upon him be blessings and peace, was in force, and among it there were those who were upon guidance before the mission of the Messiah, upon him be blessings and peace. So the general population of Yemen became Jews along with him.

Imam Muhammad ibn Ishaq related the story in full in his book (al-Sirah). The Hafiz Ibn 'Asakir wrote an extensive biography of him in his (Tarikh), and mentioned that he ruled Damascus, and he cited what has been narrated prohibiting reviling and cursing him. Ibn Kathir said: It seems, and Allah knows best, that he was a disbeliever and then embraced Islam, following the religion of Kalim (Musa) at the hands of the rabbis of the Jews of that time, who were upon the truth before the mission of the Messiah, peace be upon him. He performed the pilgrimage to the House in the time of the Jurhumites, clothed it with coverings and striped garments of silk, sacrificed six thousand camels there, glorified and honoured it. Then he returned to Yemen. Al-Hafiz Ibn 'Asakir related his story in full through many lengthy and detailed chains, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Abdullah ibn Salam, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, and Ka'b al-Ahbar, and to him is the reference in all of that, and also to 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who is the most firmly established, greatest and most knowledgeable. Likewise Wahb ibn Munabbih narrated his story, and Muhammad ibn Ishaq in (al-Sirah), as is well known there. Al-Hafiz Ibn 'Asakir was confused in some contexts between the biography of this Tubba' and the biography of another who came long after him by a great span of time. For this Tubba' referred to in the Qur'an, his people embraced Islam at his hands, then after his death they reverted to worshipping bulls and idols, so Allah the Exalted punished them, as He mentioned in Surat Saba'.

This Tubba' is Tubba' al-Awsat (the middle Tubba'). His name is As'ad Abu Karib. No one in Himyar had a longer reign than him. He died about seven hundred years before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ. They mention that when the two rabbis of the Jews of Madinah told him that this town is the place of emigration of a Prophet at the end of time whose name is Ahmad, he composed poetry about that and entrusted it to the people of Madinah. They inherited it from one another and transmitted it generation after generation. Among those who memorised it was Abu Ayyub Khalid ibn Zayd al-Ansari, in whose house the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed, and it is:

(p-5312)

I bear witness concerning Ahmad that he is a Messenger from Allah, Creator of souls,
So if my life were extended to his lifetime, I would be his minister and cousin.
And I would strive with the sword against his enemies, and relieve his breast of every grief.

Then Ibn Kathir cited reports prohibiting reviling him. In sum, his story mentioned, and what is related concerning him, even if its chain does not meet the conditions of the sound, is something that may be treated with leniency, because it is purely a report devoid of any legal ruling. Indeed, there is no doubt that Quraysh knew, from the grandeur of his report which was transmitted to them through mass transmission, what contains the greatest admonition for them; and for this reason He left out his account, referring them to what they knew of his affair and what had been talked about regarding his matter. The purpose is only admonition and taking lessons, not relating it as a mere news item or a tale told in evening gatherings, as is the secret in similar accounts. And success is from Allah.

His words ﴿in the bellies﴾ are like His words: ﴿the Fire of Allah, kindled﴾ [al-Humazah: 6] ﴿which rises over the hearts﴾ [al-Humazah: 7]. And this verse is like the verse in al-Saffat: ﴿Is that better as a welcome, or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ [al-Saffat: 62] ﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Saffat: 63] ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs from the root of the Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 64] ﴿its emerging fruit is as though it were the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat: 65] ﴿Indeed, they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it﴾ [al-Saffat: 66] ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of scalding water﴾ [al-Saffat: 67].

(p-5314) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[47] ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾

﴿Seize him and drag him﴾ means: push him violently. ﴿Into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ means: into its center and its heart.

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[48] ﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of the scalding water.﴾

﴿Then pour over his head some of the torment of the scalding water.﴾ That is: so that it reaches and strikes all parts of his body.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

[49] ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble.﴾

﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble.﴾ That is: it is said to him this, by way of mockery and derision, so that there is completed for him, along with the first punishment, which is the sensory (ḥissī) punishment, the intellectual (ʿaqlī) punishment.

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted: [50] ﴿Indeed, this is what you used to doubt.﴾

﴿Indeed, this﴾ — i.e., the punishment, or the matter: ﴿what you used to doubt﴾ — i.e., you used to be in doubt, despite the clear evidence for it; or you used to dispute and contend with one another about it.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[51] ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure place.﴾

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in a secure place.﴾ That is: its occupant will be safe from fear and dread.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[52, 53] ﴿In gardens and springs﴾ ﴿they will wear of fine silk and brocade, facing one another﴾ [al-Dukhan: 53].

(p-5315) ﴿In gardens and springs﴾ ﴿they will wear of fine silk and brocade﴾ [al-Dukhan: 53]: i.e., of silk that is thin and that is thick. ﴿Facing one another﴾ [al-Dukhan: 53]: i.e., in their assemblies or their places, owing to the fine arrangement of the chambers and the orderly disposition of their dwellings.

**On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[54] ﴿Thus. And We shall pair them with fair ones, with wide, lovely eyes.﴾

﴿Thus. And We shall pair them with fair ones, with wide, lovely eyes.﴾ That is: We join them with that which brings delight to their eyes and comfort to their hearts, by their reaching what they love and attaining the fullness of their desires.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55] ﴿They call for every kind of fruit therein, secure.﴾

﴿They call for every kind of fruit therein, secure.﴾ That is: they ask for and command the bringing of whatever fruits they desire, secure from every harm.
